findings.headline: Council carrying unquantified Equal Pay claim relating to over 400 employees transferred from former County Council
findings.detail: The council received an Equal Pay claim in August 2023 relating to over 400 employees of the former County Council now employed by Cumberland. The report notes 'the council is carrying risk from an Equal Pay claim' but the financial impact is unquantified.
findings.matters: Equal pay claims can result in substantial backdated pay awards. An unquantified contingent liability is a hidden risk to the budget, particularly if the claim is settled while the council is managing large deficits.
findings.figures: 400+ employees affected; amount unquantified
findings.quote: receipt in August 2023 by the council and Westmorland & Furness Council of an Equal Pay claim relating to over 400 employees of the former County Council now employed by the council which the council is taking steps to minimise

findings.headline: General Fund reserves are only just above minimum required; asset sales yield insufficient and behind schedule
findings.detail: General Fund reserves: 31.3.27 estimated at £26.51m (vs £26.15m in 2023). Expected asset sales yields: £1.3m (2025-26), £2.76m (2026-27), £6.07m (2027-28). CIPFA concludes: 'reserves are low and not significantly increasing' and 'asset sales are insufficient to significantly increase reserves.'
findings.matters: Low reserves with no buffer leaves the council vulnerable to any variance in spending or income. Asset sales are the only planned reserve replenishment and they are materializing slowly.
findings.figures: General Fund reserves: £26.51m (near minimum); asset sales: £1.3-6.07m annually planned
findings.quote: Though the council has preserved the overall level of reserves, the general fund is only just above the minimum required and though they are accelerating, asset sales are insufficient to significantly increase reserves.

findings.headline: SEND identified as 'the most significant long-term financial risk' with no fully implemented sufficiency solution
findings.detail: CIPFA notes SEND cost pressures are 'largely outside short-term control' due to EHCP growth, insufficient local provision, and high transport costs. The council remains dependent on external market provision. Costs are likely to continue to increase without accelerated delivery of local provision.
findings.matters: SEND is nationally a growing cost pressure; a council admitting it lacks control suggests this line item will continue to be a budget pressure and potential overspend source.
findings.figures: SEND and inclusion pressures drove Q3 2025-26 children's overspend; 56% of 2026-27 children's budget taken by placements and SEND transport
findings.quote: SEND represents the most significant long-term financial risk to the council.

findings.headline: May 2027 council elections will change leadership at the moment the most difficult budget decisions are required
findings.detail: CIPFA notes: 'whole council elections will take place in May 2027 it is critical that by the end of 2026 there is a credible and costed plan to bridge the budget gaps.' Later: 'the budget gaps for 2028-29 and 2029-30 will require some difficult political choices in a situation where the elections of May 2027 may deliver a new inexperienced leadership for the council.'
findings.matters: Leadership change during fiscal crisis creates risk of policy reversal, delayed decisions, or loss of corporate knowledge at a critical moment.
findings.figures: Elections May 2027; budget decisions needed by end-2026; gaps arise 2028-29 and 2029-30 after changeover
findings.quote: whole council elections will take place in May 2027 it is critical that by the end of 2026 there is a credible and costed plan to bridge the budget gaps detailed in the MTFP for 2027-28

findings.headline: Council has no appetite for the tax increases and service cuts required to close the budget gap for 2028-29 and beyond
findings.detail: The report states: 'the council has no appetite to seek increases in Council Tax above the referendum threshold and there is no plan to cease any discretionary services, which will be needed to close the budget gap for 2028-29.' This gap of £50-60m cannot be filled by savings or asset sales alone without service reductions or tax rises.
findings.matters: Political unwillingness to take difficult decisions, combined with a £50m+ gap, signals the council may face a second or third EFS request rather than solving the problem structurally.
findings.figures: Gap 2028-29: £50.85m; 2029-30: £59.51m; no mechanism identified to bridge these
findings.quote: the council has no appetite to seek increases in Council Tax above the referendum threshold and there is no plan to cease any discretionary services, which will be needed to close the budget gap for 2028-29.

findings.headline: External audit found over half of internal audit reviews had partial assurance or lower, suggesting pervasive control weakness
findings.detail: In November 2025, External Audit noted that 'at June 2025, more than half of the reviews for the year had partial assurance or lower. They suggested that internal control weakness may be pervasive.' This is a governance red flag indicating systemic control defects.
findings.matters: Pervasive internal control weaknesses reduce confidence in financial reporting, budget management, and the council's ability to execute plans reliably.
findings.figures: More than 50% of internal audit reviews: partial assurance or lower
findings.quote: at June 2025, more than half of the reviews for the year had partial assurance or lower. They suggested that internal control weakness may be pervasive.

findings.headline: Transformation programme has not moved 'as far and as fast' as planned, with headcount growing not shrinking
findings.detail: Despite significant EFS investment in transformation, headcount grew from 4,085 (April 2023) to 4,472 (April 2026). Delays were encountered in waste collection and children's services savings. CIPFA notes: 'The council has not moved as far and as fast as it originally set out to do on its transformation programme.'
findings.matters: A slipping transformation programme undermines the council's ability to deliver the £67m recurring savings it has built into its MTFP. Cost reduction efforts are not materializing on schedule.
findings.figures: Headcount growth: 4,085 (April 2023) → 4,472 (April 2026); planned savings £67.05m recurring but not on track
findings.quote: The council has not moved as far and as fast as it originally set out to do on its transformation programme. Delays were encountered in waste collection and children's savings.

findings.headline: Council acknowledges it has a structural deficit and faces a funding cliff-edge after 2028-29
findings.detail: In February 2026, the council told the Executive that 'the future funding system now assumes greater local self-financing, particularly through council tax with the risk of a funding cliff edge after 2028-29.' The council has argued to government that it has a structural deficit where cost growth exceeds funding growth.
findings.matters: Structural deficits are by definition not fixed by one-off savings. This signals fundamental imbalance between the council's cost base and its funding envelope that may require service reductions or tax rises beyond the council's current appetite.
findings.figures: Structural deficit framed as growth of £30-27m per year vs savings of £0.63-2.39m
findings.quote: the council argues that it has a structural deficit, where increase in funding is not meeting increase in un-avoidable and LGR related costs.

findings.headline: Total borrowing increased from £243.87m to £282.12m in nine months, with unsupported borrowing in capital programme continuing to grow
findings.detail: June 2024 borrowing: £243.87m; Q3 2025-26: £282.12m. The capital programme continues to grow despite governance efforts. Unsupported (prudential) borrowing in the future programme: £189.67m. The report notes 'the size of the capital programme has continued to climb and requires higher borrowing to fund it.'
findings.matters: Rapid growth in debt service obligations worsens the council's fiscal trajectory and reduces headroom to address revenue pressures. Unitary council average is £417m, so Cumberland is not yet at the top, but the direction is adverse.
findings.figures: Borrowing growth: £243.87m (June 2024) → £282.12m (Q3 2025-26); Unsupported borrowing in future programme: £189.67m
findings.quote: the size of the capital programme has continued to climb and requires higher borrowing to fund it.

findings.headline: Council has used Emergency Financial Support to balance budgets for three consecutive years with no expectation of repayment
findings.detail: Over three full years, the council has relied on EFS and reserves to achieve balanced budgets. For 2026-27, the council is using EFS of £11.83m (subject to approval). The report states: 'There is no apparent expectation of an ability to pay back the EFS received.' This signals structural deficit, not cyclical difficulty.
findings.matters: EFS dependency without a repayment plan indicates the council cannot cover its operating costs from revenue, a fundamental solvency concern for lenders.
findings.figures: Total EFS approved 2023-24 to 2025-26: £56.65m; 2026-27: £11.83m re-profiling requested
findings.quote: There is no apparent expectation of an ability to pay back the EFS received.

findings.headline: Children's services has repeatedly overspent its budget by £10-17m annually with no structural fix in place
findings.detail: Q3 2025-26 projected overspend: £10.74m. In 2023-24, the service overspent by £17.04m; in 2024-25, it spent £90.95m against a £72.31m budget. At the last budget-setting deadline, the Director of Children's Services invoked statutory authority to say the proposed budget was insufficient, forcing emergency action.
findings.matters: Persistent and large overspends in a demand-led service suggest structural cost pressures the council cannot control, making budget forecasting unreliable and future deficits likely.
findings.figures: Q3 2025-26 expected overspend £10.74m; 2023-24 £17.04m overspend; 2024-25 £18.64m overspend (£90.95m spend vs £72.31m budget)
findings.quote: At the 11th hour of setting the 2026-27 budget, the Director of Children's Services invoked his statutory responsibility to suggest the budget was insufficient.

findings.headline: Budget gaps of £25.57m (2027-28), £50.85m (2028-29) and £59.51m (2029-30) with only £2.39m-£0.63m savings identified
findings.detail: The council's Medium-Term Financial Plan reveals growing deficits across the forecast period. Savings proposals are negligible compared to the scale of the gaps. The council has no definitive plan to meet these gaps, which is identified as the council's highest-rated risk (rating 9).
findings.matters: A lender would be alarmed by the scale of the shortfall and the absence of credible bridging strategy, raising questions about financial sustainability beyond 2027-28.
findings.figures: 2027-28: £25.57m gap vs £2.39m savings; 2028-29: £50.85m gap vs £0.63m savings; 2029-30: £59.51m gap vs £0.63m savings
findings.quote: The budget gaps will be 2027-28 - £25.57million; 2028-29 - £50.85 million; 2029-30 - £59.51 million.

An October 2025 audit gave Limited assurance on H&S policies. Multiple control activities with July 2026 deadlines remained incomplete at August review.

findings.detail: Current workforce capacity is insufficient for demand, creating waiting lists and delaying allocation. Risk is currently 20 (Major x Very Likely), target 9. Service is performing (96.4% of families not escalating to statutory care) but under stress.

findings.figures: Risk score 20 (Major x Very Likely); 96.4% of families not escalating to statutory social care
findings.quote: Demand continues to exceed available practitioner resource, resulting in waiting lists and delays in allocation for some families.

findings.headline: Cared For children placement costs inflating faster than internal capacity expansion relieves pressure
findings.detail: The council faces tight control of the Cared For budget, but this is being offset by rising per-unit costs for external residential provision. New internal children's homes are projected to come on stream from end of 26/27 through 27/28. Until then, the council remains dependent on expensive external placements while managing budget tightly. Risk score is 15 (Most Severe x Possible).
findings.matters: A demand-led service where unit costs are rising faster than internal capacity replaces external provision creates unsustainable budget pressure; the funding solution (internal homes) is still 12+ months away
findings.figures: Risk score 15 (Most Severe x Possible); new homes from end of 26/27 through 27/28
findings.quote: This is offset by the growing unit cost of external residential provision.

findings.headline: Under-borrowed position increased by £19.4m while capital expenditure was reprofiled, suggesting cash constraints or deliberate liquidity management
findings.detail: The council's under-borrowed position (the gap between the Capital Financing Requirement and actual borrowing) increased from £86.017m to £105.418m. This occurred despite budgeting for unfinanced capital expenditure of £107.366m and means the council deferred £105.4m of borrowing that could have been taken. Combined with the £185.5m capital expenditure reprofiling, this pattern suggests either strong cash generation that allowed the council to avoid borrowing at elevated rates, or financial caution/constraint requiring use of reserves.
findings.matters: An increasing under-borrowed position while capital is being reprofiled could indicate the council is managing cash tightly or facing constraints that prevent full capital delivery. Conversely, if the council has strong cash flows, this strategy is sensible given PWLB rates rose to 6.29% (25-year) during the year. However, the combination raises questions: is the reprofiling of capital being driven by lack of cash to fund borrowing?
findings.figures: Under-borrowed £105.418m at 31 March 2026 vs £86.017m at 31 March 2025 (increase of £19.401m); borrowing requirement £386.938m but actual borrowing £281.520m
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, the level of under borrowing stood at £105.418m compared to £86.017 at 31 March 2025.

findings.headline: LOBO loan carries 7.55% interest rate, substantially higher than current market rates, creating potential refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council holds two LOBO loans (Lender Option Borrower Option loans). One carries a 7.55% fixed rate, which is approximately 180 basis points above current PWLB 10-year rates (5.72%) and significantly above the council's average borrowing rate (3.80%). The report provides no information on when these loans were taken, when lender options can be exercised, or what would happen if refinancing were required.
findings.matters: LOBO loans carry embedded refinancing risk. If the lender exercises their call option, the council would need to refinance the £16m loan at potentially much higher rates than currently budgeted. The 7.55% rate suggests either very old debt taken at historical highs, or underlying credit/counterparty concerns. The lack of detail on these loans' terms and risks is a gap in this report.
findings.figures: LOBO principal £16.000m at rates 4.45% and 7.55%; total council borrowing £281.520m at weighted average 3.80%
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026 the Council had two Lender Option Borrower Option (LOBO) loans. The interest rates on these loans are 4.45% and 7.55%.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure plan was reprofiled by £185.5m (37% of original budget) during the year with reasons unexplained
findings.detail: The council approved £298.5m capital expenditure for 2025-26 but revised the budget to £191.7m during the year, and achieved £186.5m. The reprofiling moved £185.5m to 2026-27 and beyond. The reasons for this substantial revision and the timing of reprofiling during the year are not explained in the report, raising questions about the realism of the initial budget and the council's capital delivery capacity.
findings.matters: Significant reprofiling of capital expenditure affects service delivery timing, future borrowing needs, and cash forecasting. A lender needs to understand whether this reflects normal budget management or indicates project delays, funding constraints, or overambitious planning that could affect the council's ability to deliver planned services and generate expected revenues.
findings.figures: Approved £298.505m, reprofiled £185.502m, actual £186.506m (62% outturn rate on original budget)
findings.quote: reprofiling adjustments moving capital expenditure of £185.502m from 2025-26 to 2026-27 (£144.189m) and future years (£41.313m)

findings.detail: The report states asset register work 'remains consistent and is being updated to Concerto' but notes 'Identification of legacy issues by HSE and Ridge reports relating to H&S and building compliance issues' (12 Aug 2026). findings.paper_title: Risk Management Progress Report – August 2026 Appendix 2 (FULL REPORT)
findings.headline: Children's Services Academy Model funding is uncertain beyond March 2027, creating recruitment risk for newly qualified social workers
findings.detail: Two separate risk entries (SRR-16-04 and SRR-04-01) flag the same issue: 'Funding for the Academy Model has not been agreed past March 2027. This poses a significant risk to the recruitment of newly qualified Social Workers.' The Academy Model is described as 'embedded for newly qualified social workers to join the workforce' and the council notes 'Apprenticeship offer live with 5 applications confirmed for 2025, this needs to increase to 10.' Loss of funding would halt a key pipeline during a period of national staffing shortage.
findings.matters: Staffing instability in statutory children's services creates service delivery and audit risk. A freeze on newly qualified recruits during national shortage conditions would intensify reliance on agency and overseas recruitment, both costly and less stable.

findings.quote: Funding for the Academy Model has not been agreed past March 2027. This poses a significant risk to the recruitment of newly qualified Social Workers.

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Progress Report – August 2026 Appendix 2 (FULL REPORT)
findings.headline: Children's Services external residential placement costs are growing while internal capacity remains under development
findings.detail: The council reports 'tighter control and monitoring' of cared-for budgets but notes that 'growing unit cost of external residential provision' offsets controls. Projects to open internal homes are 'progressing and within timeframe' with homes 'beginning to come on stream from end of 26/27 through to 27/28'. The council received a £908,980 DfE grant for a two-bedroom complex-needs home and has redesignated Blackwell Rd from emergency to mainstream provision (expanding from 2 to 5 beds), but headline risk remains the 'growing unit cost' of placements while internal alternatives develop.
findings.matters: External residential provision is typically the highest-cost placement type for children's services. Growing unit costs during a wait for internal capacity to come online creates budget risk in 2026/27 before savings materialise.
findings.figures: £908,980 DfE grant; Blackwell Rd expanded from 2 beds to 5 beds; homes coming on stream 'from end of 26/27 through to 27/28'
findings.quote: There is tighter control and monitoring of the direction of travel on the Cared For budget and the number of children in Cared For placements. This is offset by the growing unit cost of external residential provision.

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Progress Report – August 2026 Appendix 4
findings.headline: Annual budget risk articulation incomplete and five months overdue with no recovery plan.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton recommended that risks identified in the annual budget report be sufficiently detailed and consistent with the strategic risk register format, targeted for March 2026. As of August 2026, the required liaison between the Risk Manager and the Section 151 finance officers remains outstanding with no agreed timescale established.
findings.matters: When annual budgets do not explicitly articulate the risks identified against proposals, budget decisions proceed without adequate risk visibility, making it difficult to assess whether the council is making properly informed financial decisions.
findings.figures: Original target date 13/03/26; five months overdue as of August 2026
findings.quote: Ensuring risks identified in the annual budget report are sufficiently detailed, with mitigation and consistent with the SRR revised format. Liaison required with Chief Finance Officer (Section 151) and Senior Manager Finance (Deputy S151). RM to identify timescales and liaise. This is still outstanding.

findings.headline: Internal audit assessment is 'Partial assurance' on planning service controls, with three high-priority recommendations
findings.detail: Audit opinion of 'Partial assurance' indicates insufficient control to ensure service objectives are achieved. Three high-priority recommendations address: (1) system integration across three separate non-integrated planning platforms (IDOX, Arcus, legacy system); (2) frequent performance reporting to replace quarterly cycles; (3) formal action plan to address application backlog.
findings.matters: Partial assurance on a statutory, high-impact service signals material control weaknesses. Combined with documented statutory non-compliance and performance deterioration, this indicates management lacks real-time visibility and control.
findings.figures: 3 High priority recommendations; 4 Medium priority; Partial assurance (two levels below Reasonable)
findings.quote: From the areas examined and tested as part of this audit review, we consider the current controls operating within Planning (Service Standards) provides Partial assurance.

findings.headline: Planning service is operating with a 10-15% staffing shortfall and relying extensively on temporary agency resources
findings.detail: Management reports capacity shortfall of approximately 10-15% against estimated staffing requirements. To mitigate, the service relies extensively on EPW (external temporary staff) resources. Recent graduate recruitment is underway, with two additional graduate planners due to commence in September 2026.
findings.matters: Persistent understaffing of a growth-critical service is an operational stress indicator. Dependency on temporary labour is costlier and less stable than permanent staffing, suggesting financial pressure and risk of service degradation.
findings.figures: 10-15% staffing shortfall; 2 graduate planners due September 2026
findings.quote: Information provided by management indicates that the Planning Service is currently operating with a resource shortfall of approximately 10% to 15% against its estimated staffing requirements.

findings.headline: Planning service performance deteriorated sharply in Q4 2025/26, with major application completion dropping from 90% to 43%
findings.detail: Quarterly performance shows significant decline across all metrics between Q3 and Q4. Major applications determined within 13 weeks fell from 90% to 43% against a target of 80%; minor applications from 90% to 77% against target 90%; householder applications from 95% to 89% against target 90%.
findings.matters: Planning enables economic growth and housing delivery—stated strategic council priorities. Sharp performance collapse indicates underlying operational stress and capacity problems that will likely persist without intervention.
findings.figures: Major Q4 43% vs Q3 90%; Minor Q4 77% vs Q3 90%; Householder Q4 89% vs Q3 95%
findings.quote: Major planning applications completed in 13 weeks 94% 89% 90% 43%; Minor Planning Applications completed in 8 weeks 90% 91% 90% 77%

findings.headline: More than half of planning applications have exceeded statutory determination timescales, creating exposure to fee refunds under the Planning Guarantee
findings.detail: As of 8 July 2026, 496 applications awaited determination. Of these, 265 (53%) had exceeded expected timescales. In Allerdale specifically, 45 of 69 applications (65%) with agreed time extensions also exceeded their revised deadlines. The Planning Guarantee allows applicants to claim fee refunds when statutory or agreed timescales are missed; the audit scope explicitly excluded quantifying this financial exposure.
findings.matters: Planning fees contribute significant revenue to service delivery. Systematic failure to meet statutory timescales creates exposure to refund obligations—an unbudgeted financial outflow that management has not quantified.
findings.figures: 265 of 496 applications (53%) overdue; 45 of 69 applications with extensions (65%) exceeded revised deadline
findings.quote: A snapshot review of all open applications across the three IT systems as of 8 July 2026 identified 496 pending applications. Of these, 265 applications (53%) had exceeded the expected decision timescales.

findings.headline: MHCLG has set a tight deadline for demonstrating progress; a written report is due by end of September 2026.
findings.detail: The council and Section 151 Officer are required to provide a written progress report to MHCLG by end of September 2026 setting out progress against each recommendation, implementation concerns, financial position updates, and actions to minimise future EFS dependency. MHCLG will continue monitoring both implementation and the council's wider governance and financial position.
findings.matters: A lender watches government oversight intensity; tight deadlines and ongoing monitoring suggest the government views Cumberland as a higher-risk authority requiring close supervision.
findings.figures: Report due 30 September 2026
findings.quote: The Council and the Section 151 Officer are required to provide a written progress report to MHCLG by the end of September 2026

findings.headline: The council lacks a comprehensive costed plan for long-term financial sustainability beyond 2027-28.
findings.detail: The review highlights the need for a more comprehensive and costed plan to achieve long-term financial sustainability. Management intends to strengthen medium-term financial planning and develop a more comprehensive programme of savings proposals for 2027-28 and beyond.
findings.matters: Absence of a detailed, costed sustainability plan suggests financial planning is reactive rather than strategic; future deficits could emerge without warning.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: The need for a more comprehensive and costed plan to achieve long-term financial sustainability

findings.headline: Substantial workforce restructuring is required but carries significant execution risk.
findings.detail: The council must deliver substantial transformation and workforce restructuring to meet its financial targets. Restructuring is costly, takes time, and can generate service disruption if not carefully managed. The council intends to continue implementing workforce restructuring funded through approved EFS.
findings.matters: Large-scale restructuring is high-risk; poor execution wastes the EFS investment and fails to deliver the savings assumed in the budget plan.
findings.figures: Funding already approved within the EFS envelope, but quantum of restructuring not stated
findings.quote: The need to deliver substantial transformation and workforce restructuring

findings.headline: CIPFA has issued 24 recommendations, several assessed as high risk and requiring urgent action during 2026-27.
findings.detail: The review produces 24 recommendations across financial management, sustainability, transformation, governance and leadership. Several are marked as high risk and require early implementation during the current financial year, indicating significant governance and control gaps.
findings.matters: High-risk recommendations requiring urgent action signal control weaknesses and execution risk; failure to deliver them quickly threatens the pathway to financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 24 recommendations; several marked high risk
findings.quote: Several recommendations are assessed as high risk and will require early action during 2026-27

findings.headline: The capital programme is growing and driving material new borrowing requirements.
findings.detail: The review identifies growth in both the scale of the capital programme and the associated borrowing needed to fund it as a significant financial challenge. This increases debt servicing costs and reduces financial headroom.
findings.matters: Rising capital borrowing directly increases medium-term revenue pressure and debt servicing obligations, constraining budget flexibility.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the paper
findings.quote: Growth in the capital programme and associated borrowing requirements

findings.headline: Children's Services and SEND are under continuing pressure and require external support to resolve.
findings.detail: The review highlights ongoing demand and cost pressures in Children's Services and SEND specifically, and recommends seeking external support for review of Children's Services, SEND, procurement and commissioning. These are typically high-cost, high-volatility service areas.
findings.matters: Persistent service pressures consume reserves, create unpredictable budget swings, and force difficult trade-offs across the council's portfolio.
findings.figures: Not specified in the paper
findings.quote: Continuing pressures within Children's Services and SEND

findings.headline: Large forecast budget gaps are projected from 2027-28 onwards, requiring substantial further action.
findings.detail: The CIPFA review identifies significant budget deficits in the Medium-Term Financial Plan beyond 2027-28. While the review expresses confidence in achieving a balanced budget in 2027-28 itself, this depends entirely on successful delivery of transformation and savings programmes, indicating structural funding gaps remain unresolved.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance on the council's path to financial sustainability; budget gaps persisting after EFS ends suggest ongoing dependency on government support or service cuts.
findings.figures: £11.834m EFS for 2026-27; gaps forecast from 2027-28 onwards
findings.quote: expresses a high level of confidence that Cumberland can achieve a balanced budget in 2027-28 without further EFS support, provided that planned transformation activity and savings programmes are delivered successfully

findings.headline: Historical practice of holding cash from Money Carer cards in envelopes outside normal banking arrangements
findings.detail: Cash withdrawn from Money Carer cards was held in envelopes for future expenditure outside normal banking arrangements. Management advised this practice has now ceased and monies were returned to individual accounts.
findings.matters: This demonstrates a history of non-standard financial practices circumventing normal accounting controls and raising transparency concerns.
findings.figures: None quantified
findings.quote: A historical practice was identified whereby cash withdrawn from Money Carer cards was held in envelopes for future expenditure outside normal banking arrangements.

findings.headline: Household account balances cannot be identified or reconciled to individual residents; contributions remain unequal and unclear
findings.detail: Testing was unable to identify clear balances for each resident. Contributions are noted as unequal and often unclear, increasing risk of disputes and inaccuracies. Record keeping is inconsistent, relying on manual finance books and receipts without centralised or structured records.
findings.matters: Inability to track individual balances raises governance concerns about the council's stewardship of residents' money and exposes it to disputes and accountability failures.
findings.figures: None quantified in paper
findings.quote: Testing was unable to identify clear balances within the account for each resident. Contributions are noted as unequal and often unclear, increasing the risk of disputes and inaccuracies

findings.headline: Staff lack training on financial procedures; management unaware of approved guidance, leading to misuse of household funds
findings.detail: Staff receive no formal training in financial procedures. The management team were unaware of the formally approved Cumberland Financial Procedures document. An example was identified where household funds were used to reimburse staff taxi expenses, demonstrating misunderstanding of permissible use.
findings.matters: Untrained staff and poor procedure awareness create direct risk of improper financial management and misuse of council funds.
findings.figures: One instance of household funds used to reimburse staff taxi expenses
findings.quote: Staff receive no formal training in financial procedures with a risk of inconsistent practices. An example was identified where household funds were used to reimburse staff taxi expenses.

findings.headline: No formal reconciliation process in place for household accounts; supervisors maintain records and check their own work
findings.detail: Reviews are limited to basic manual tick/check of bank statements against receipts, with no structured methodology or documented evidence. Supervisors are responsible for both maintaining financial records and performing checks on household accounts, creating no effective segregation of duties.
findings.matters: Lack of formal reconciliation and segregation of duties are fundamental control weaknesses allowing errors or misuse to go undetected in council-managed funds.
findings.figures: 11 audit recommendations identified, 2 High priority
findings.quote: No formal reconciliation process is in place. Reviews are limited to basic manual tick/check reviews of bank statements against receipts and expected income, with no structured methodology or documented evidence of review

findings.headline: Information Governance risk remains active on the risk register due to ongoing Subject Access Request workload pressures.
findings.detail: Despite the closure of the enforcement notice and audit improvement to substantial assurance, the Information Governance risk has been escalated to the Senior Leadership Team twice and remains classified as active on the risk register. The council notes that this risk 'may reduce as performance improves' but indicates that ongoing Subject Access Request workload pressures persist.
findings.matters: Ongoing workload pressures indicate the underlying capacity or process issue is not yet fully resolved despite recent staffing additions and restructuring.
findings.figures: IG Action Plan: 21 actions established, 11 complete as of 9 July 2026, remainder in progress or pending
findings.quote: The risk remains active due to ongoing SAR workload pressures, although it may reduce as performance improves.

findings.headline: Audit assurance improved from partial to substantial, but two of seven original recommendations remain only partially implemented.
findings.detail: The original February 2026 audit gave 'partial assurance' with seven recommendations (three high-graded). This follow-up audit upgraded to 'substantial assurance'. However, five of seven recommendations have been fully implemented whilst two remain partially implemented: the formal skills matrix competency assessment (scheduled to start August 2026 via one-to-one reviews) and formal quality assurance sampling of officer work (still pending implementation).
findings.matters: Partial implementation of audit recommendations means control gaps remain unresolved and internal control weaknesses have not been fully addressed.
findings.figures: 7 original recommendations: 5 fully implemented, 2 partially implemented, 0 not implemented
findings.quote: From the areas examined and tested as part of this follow-up audit review, the audit assurance opinion has been revised to substantial assurance.

findings.headline: ICO Enforcement Notice for information handling has been closed following restructuring and staffing additions.
findings.detail: The council received an Information Commissioner's Office Enforcement Notice for failures in handling Freedom of Information and Subject Access Requests. This was closed on 28 May 2026. The council responded by restructuring the Information Governance team (effective 1 March 2026), adding staff including a new IG & Disclosure Officer (18 May 2026), bringing the team to 5 staff total, and implementing seven Standard Operating Procedures.
findings.matters: An enforcement notice indicates a governance failure requiring senior management attention, but its closure and proactive remediation suggest the council has addressed root issues and is rebuilding capacity.
findings.figures: IG team restructured 1 March 2026; new IG & Disclosure Officer appointed 18 May 2026; team expanded to 5 staff; ICO Enforcement Notice closed 28 May 2026
findings.quote: Significant progress has been made with the implementation of a revised Cumberland Information Governance structure (from the 1st March 2026), supported by updated job descriptions and the transition of staff onto Cumberland contracts. Additional staffing resources have strengthened team capacity and resilience, contributing to improved performance and the successful closure of the ICO Enforcement Notice in May 2026.

findings.headline: Audit resourcing adjustments due to staff departures at Grant Thornton; ISA260 report may slip to 11 January 2027.
findings.detail: Assistant manager-level auditors have departed public sector audit, forcing resourcing adjustments to this engagement. The auditor is aiming for substantive work conclusion by end of November but the Audit Findings report may not be presented until 11 January, close to the 31 January statutory deadline.
findings.matters: Audit slippage and resource constraints on the audit team compound the council's own capacity constraints. A compressed timeline for audit findings limits time for remediation before the deadline.
findings.figures: Audit Findings report potentially 11 January 2027; statutory deadline 31 January 2027
findings.quote: Due to some assistant manager colleagues at 'in-charge' level recently deciding to move on from public sector audit, this has resulted in some resourcing adjustments to across our audits including Cumberland. We are still targeting to conclude our audit work by the end of November and update the Committee on 1 December, however, our Audit Findings (ISA260) Report may need to be presented to the Committee on 11 January.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support of £11.834m granted for 2026-27, but does not address outer-year deficits.
findings.detail: While EFS enables a balanced 2026-27 budget, it is one-off funding that does nothing to close the £25–60m structural gap ahead. The council remains structurally unbalanced.
findings.matters: EFS is a short-term liquidity solution, not a structural fix. The council required state rescue funding and still faces substantial unresolved deficits.
findings.figures: EFS: £11.834m for 2026-27; structural gaps: £25.57m to £59.51m in outer years
findings.quote: The Council has been granted £11.834 million of Exceptional Financial Support (2026-27), conditional on an external assurance review of its finances and governance by CIPFA.

findings.headline: CIPFA recommends engagement of an external facilitator to support budget-setting through 2028-29.
findings.detail: The council lacks sufficient internal capacity or confidence to set budgets in the outer years. CIPFA's recommendation for external facilitation, retained through the 2028-29 budget round, signals that officers cannot be relied upon alone to solve the problem.
findings.matters: External facilitation is a signal of governance weakness. It indicates the council requires third-party support to make the difficult decisions needed to return to balance.
findings.figures: External facilitator recommended through 2028-29
findings.quote: CIPFA recommends an external facilitator be engaged to support a balanced 2027-28 budget, retained until the 2028-29 budget is set.

findings.headline: Children's services and SEND transformation identified as a key delivery risk, compounded by workforce instability.
findings.detail: The CIPFA review flagged deliverability of children's services and SEND transformation as a core financial risk, alongside workforce instability. These are the dominant drivers of overspend across the sector but particularly challenging for this council to manage.
findings.matters: SEND and children's spending is difficult to control and has been a material driver of this council's deficit. If transformation plans fail, the deficit gap will worsen materially.
findings.figures: Identified as key risk in CIPFA review
findings.quote: In common with a number of local authorities, key risks include the deliverability of children's services and SEND transformation and workforce instability.

findings.headline: Persistent VFM (value for money) weaknesses in financial sustainability, governance, and efficiency, continuing from 2024-25.
findings.detail: The auditor's risk assessment identified ongoing risks of significant weakness across all three VFM criteria (financial sustainability, governance, and economy/efficiency), the same weaknesses reported in the prior year. Additional audit work is required to address this.
findings.matters: Continuing weakness in VFM arrangements means the council has not fixed underlying problems from the prior year. A lender is exposed to repeated governance failures.
findings.figures: Three VFM criteria all flagged with significant weakness
findings.quote: Our risk assessment regarding your arrangements to secure value for money in its use of resources identified ongoing risks of significant weakness across all three criteria (as reported in our 2024-25 VFM work), requiring additional work.

findings.headline: Structural deficits of £25.57m, £50.85m, and £59.51m in years 2027-28 through 2029-30, with no definitive savings plan in place.
findings.detail: The CIPFA review, a condition of receiving Exceptional Financial Support for 2026-27, found that while the council can balance 2027-28, deficits then expand sharply in outer years. The review explicitly notes no definitive savings plan exists to close these gaps.
findings.matters: These are material deficits, each larger than the prior year, with no identified solution. A lender cannot rely on the council managing out of the problem; without a plan, these will require further intervention.
findings.quote: gaps then widen sharply to £25.57m (2027-28), £50.85m (2028-29) and £59.51m (2029-30), with no definitive savings plan yet in place to close them.

findings.headline: Clean audit opinion not expected until November 2031, five years away.
findings.detail: The auditor is establishing a 'pathway to recovery' rather than moving toward a standard opinion. The council's financial statements require multi-year rebuilding of assurance before reaching an unqualified opinion. This signals serious underlying accounting or control weaknesses.
findings.matters: A lender depends on reliable financial statements; delayed recovery of audit opinion indicates the council's books are not in a state of trust, and the timeline extends well beyond what would be typical.
findings.figures: Unqualified opinion target: November 2031
findings.quote: a proposed route to an unqualified "clean" opinion by November 2031. This pathway may be reduced depending on the extent to which a full in-year audit can be performed in this and subsequent years.

findings.headline: No documented definition of desired culture or SMART objectives to measure culture change
findings.detail: Although cultural themes are discussed informally and staff feedback is captured via the Pulse Survey, the council has not formally documented what its desired culture should look like or set specific, measurable objectives to achieve it. Culture development is characterized as 'broadly reactive, rather than proactive,' making progress assessment unclear.
findings.matters: For a reorganized council integrating four separate organizations, unmeasured culture change creates risk of drift and ineffective execution on strategic objectives
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The Council does not have a documented set of workplace culture objectives necessary for progress towards the future culture state. Development of the Council's culture is broadly reactive, rather than proactive.

findings.headline: People and Culture Board did not meet for approximately 6 months, meaning governance of culture development was not routinely demonstrated
findings.detail: The board established to act as the primary governance forum for culture development had not convened for 6 months as of the May 2026 audit date. During this period management described oversight as only 'informally retained.' The board has since reconvened but the gap reveals governance weakness in a post-reorganization integration area.
findings.matters: Culture integration after local government reorganization affects the council's ability to execute its strategic plan; active governance of this is material
findings.figures: 6-month meeting gap as of May 2026
findings.quote: At the time of audit (May 2026), Board Terms of Reference were not finalised, and the Board had not met for approximately 6 months. As the Board had not met for a considerable period of time, it was not possible to demonstrate that organisational culture development was being routinely overseen, coordinated and challenged.

findings.headline: Exit interview process implementation delayed 7 months past agreed deadline
findings.detail: A high-priority recommendation from a previous audit to implement a revised leavers and exit interview process was agreed for 31 January 2026 but remains unimplemented as of the August 2026 audit completion. The process is awaiting final approval. This affects the council's ability to capture data on why staff are leaving, which is material for a post-reorganization council's stability.
findings.matters: Staff retention and understanding leaver reasons is critical for a reorganized council; a 7-month miss on a high-priority previous recommendation suggests execution or governance weakness
findings.figures: Agreed implementation date 31 January 2026; audit completed 28 August 2026 (7 months overdue)
findings.quote: The revised leavers and exit interview process has not yet been implemented. The new approach is awaiting final approval before it can go live.

findings.headline: Business continuity arrangements have failed, affecting partnership function
findings.detail: Audit noted that unplanned absence of a key Steering Group member contributed to a reduction in business continuity, and the partnership has not maintained resilience arrangements as expected. No documented succession planning or contingency arrangements are in place.
findings.matters: If the partnership cannot function when key individuals are absent, the council's investment and its role as accountable body are at risk of disruption.
findings.figures: At least 1 unplanned absence of a key member caused governance disruption
findings.quote: It is noted that unplanned absence of a key Steering Group Member may have contributed to a reduction in business continuity. Resilience arrangements are necessary to help ensure that the Partnership continues to function in line with the agreed Constitution, should a key Member be absent.

findings.headline: Partnership governance meetings have not been held as required
findings.detail: The draft Partnership Constitution requires at least 4 Steering Group meetings per year and one Annual General Meeting per year. No AGM has been held since 2023, and the last Steering Group meeting was November 2025. This represents a failure to maintain basic governance structures.
findings.matters: Without regular governance meetings and annual general meetings, there is no structured oversight of how the partnership operates or how council funding is being deployed.
findings.figures: No AGM since 2023; last Steering Group meeting November 2025
findings.quote: The draft Partnership Constitution details that an Annual General Meeting must be held once a year to present a report of Social Enterprise Partnership work and elect Steering Group Membership (for a period of 3 AGMs). No AGM has been held since 2023. The draft Constitution also requires at least 4 Steering Group meetings per year. The last meeting was held in November 2025.

findings.headline: Council invests in a partnership with no formal governance agreement
findings.detail: Cumberland Council contributes approximately £27,000 core funding plus accumulated ear-marked reserves to the Social Enterprise Partnership, but there is no formal written agreement between the council and the partnership defining accountability, roles, responsibilities, or governance arrangements. Audit states this informal arrangement increases uncertainty over accountability, decision-making, liabilities and ownership of outcomes.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether council resources committed to external entities are subject to proper governance oversight and accountability frameworks.
findings.figures: approximately £27,000 core funding from Cumberland Council, supplemented using accumulated ear-marked reserves
findings.quote: There is no formal partnership arrangement in place between Cumberland Council and the unincorporated (no separate legal personality) Social Enterprise Partnership. Cumberland Council contributes officer time, support, influence and funding to the Partnership. The current informal arrangement increases uncertainty over accountability, decision-making, liabilities, and ownership of outcomes.

findings.headline: Risk-based assurance audits cut by 87 days, from 434 to 347 days
findings.detail: Risk-based assurance covers reviews across service areas where audit has identified the greatest need. The revised plan cuts this category by 20%, the largest single reduction in audit coverage.
findings.matters: This category is how internal audit targets resources at areas of highest risk. A reduction of 87 days means fewer service areas will be audited for control effectiveness this year.
findings.figures: 434 days originally planned; 347 days in revised plan
findings.quote: Risk Based Assurance Reviews Reviews that have been identified across service areas following a risk assessment to ensure that Internal Audit resources are targeted at the areas where the greatest benefit will be achieved. 370 434 347

findings.headline: Strategic risk audit on cost of living was cancelled
findings.detail: A planned audit of management controls around cost-of-living strategic risk was cancelled and removed from the plan. This audit would have assessed whether the council is actively embedding controls for this identified risk.
findings.matters: Cost-of-living pressures are a material operational and financial risk for councils. Cancelling oversight of this area suggests it is not a priority for internal audit, or resources are too constrained to cover it.
findings.figures: 13 audit days cancelled
findings.quote: Cost of Living (Strategic Risk) Review management of strategic risk to ensure effective and actively embedded controls are in place. AR Cancel 13 -13 0

findings.headline: 160 audit days from 2025/26 still incomplete, consuming a quarter of the 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The audit team allocated all 160 contingency days to finish 2025/26 work. This means the team either under-delivered or was over-committed last year. In 2026/27 they have only 1,844 days available for new planned work across the entire council.
findings.matters: It signals audit resource constraints at a time when oversight of financial controls matters most. A lender needs confidence that the council's internal control framework is being properly monitored.
findings.figures: 2004 available audit days in 2026/27; 160 days allocated to complete 2025/26 work
findings.quote: 2025/26 Internal Audit Plan Time required to complete Audit work from previous financial year Con Final 0 160 160

findings.headline: Assurance opinion remains only Reasonable, not Substantial, reflecting ongoing control weaknesses
findings.detail: The audit assurance opinion improved from Partial to Reasonable between 2024 and 2026. However, the S151 Officer notes that 'a number of key actions remain outstanding, particularly around risk management, policy approval, staff training, and debt reporting,' and emphasizes that completion within agreed timescales is necessary to 'strengthen governance, improve debt recovery arrangements, and reduce the Council's exposure to financial risk.'
findings.matters: A Reasonable Assurance opinion (vs. Substantial or Comprehensive) indicates material gaps in internal control design or application; paired with multiple missed deadlines, it signals the council has not yet remediated prior audit findings.
findings.figures: 1 high-priority recommendation outstanding; 4 medium-priority recommendations outstanding
findings.quote: However, a number of key actions remain outstanding, particularly around risk management, policy approval, staff training, and debt reporting. It is important that these actions are completed within the agreed timescales to strengthen governance, improve debt recovery arrangements, and reduce the Council's exposure to financial risk.

findings.headline: System development delays are now linked to resource and skills constraints, pushing implementation to March 2027
findings.detail: Work to develop enhanced aged debt reporting through Power BI has been delayed due to resource and skills constraints. The original ContrOCC aged debt module was found impractical and a replacement approach through Power BI is underway, but the new implementation date is 31st March 2027—over two years after the original recommendation.
findings.matters: A lender depends on councils' ability to monitor and recover receivables; system delays and resource constraints that prevent debt reporting indicate material operational fragility in a material function.
findings.figures: Original deadline December 2025; revised deadline March 2027
findings.quote: Progress has been delayed due to resource and skills constraints. Work is now underway to develop enhanced reporting through Power BI to support improved debt monitoring and targeted recovery.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care debt management procedure remains unapproved 13 months after original deadline
findings.detail: A draft ASC Debt Management and Recovery Procedure was completed and aligned with corporate policy, but formal approval from the S151 Officer was expected by end of July 2026—now past due. The procedure is described as lacking explicit requirements for documented options appraisals when cases escalate to Legal Services, reducing assurance of consistent decision-making.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is a material budget line and debt recovery is a control function; unfinalized procedures and approval delays suggest governance uncertainty in a significant risk area.
findings.figures: Procedure drafted 28th August 2026; approval deadline was 31st December 2025 (original) and end July 2026 (revised)
findings.quote: The only remaining action is to incorporate minor amendments and obtain formal approval from the Section 151 Officer, which management expects to complete by the end of July 2026.

findings.headline: High-priority debt risks are not formally recorded in the council's risk management system
findings.detail: The audit identified that Community Finance debt is subject to management oversight through the Debt Steering Group, but key risks have not been formally documented on the council's risk management system or linked to operational and strategic risk registers. This is classified as a high-priority recommendation with significant risk exposure including increased debt, errors, and financial losses.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that a council formally manages and monitors material financial risks; informal oversight is insufficient for portfolio exposure to Community Finance debt.
findings.figures: 1 high-priority recommendation for formal risk recording and documentation
findings.quote: Community Finance debt is subject to management oversight including the Debt Steering Group; however, key risks have not been formally recorded on the Council's risk management system or linked to operational and strategic risk registers.

findings.headline: Family Hubs and Start for Life cross-cutting programme audit cancelled.
findings.detail: Family Hubs & Start for Life Programme (Cross-cutting), allocated 18 days, is marked as Cancel Proposed. This was a cross-directorate programme audit that has been removed from the plan.
findings.matters: Cross-cutting programmes represent integration risk. Cancelling audit of a major early-help programme removes oversight of how directorates are delivering it together.
findings.figures: Family Hubs & Start for Life Programme: 18 days allocated, cancelled
findings.quote: Family Hubs & Start for Life Programme (Cross-cutting) 18 0 AR Cancel Proposed

findings.headline: Demand management audit in adult social care has been cancelled.
findings.detail: The Demand (Transition Arrangements) audit under Adult Social Care & Housing, allocated 18 days, is marked as Cancel Proposed. This was intended to audit demand forecasting and transition arrangements.
findings.matters: Adult social care demand is a core driver of budget pressures and service delivery risk. Cancelling an audit of demand arrangements removes oversight of a high-risk area.
findings.figures: Demand (Transition Arrangements): 18 days allocated, cancelled
findings.quote: Demand (Transition Arrangements) 18 0 AR Cancel Proposed

findings.headline: Cost of Living strategic risk audit has been cancelled rather than conducted.
findings.detail: The Cost of Living (Strategic Risk) audit, allocated 13 days, is marked as Cancel Proposed. This was intended as a strategic risk review but has been removed from the audit plan.
findings.matters: Cancelling a strategic risk audit on cost of living—a major driver of council budget pressure—suggests either the risk is not being formally assessed, or audit resources were constrained and this was deprioritised.
findings.figures: Cost of Living (Strategic Risk): 13 days allocated, cancelled
findings.quote: Cost of Living (Strategic Risk) 13 0 AR Cancel Proposed

findings.headline: Planning audit returned Partial assurance, indicating only some controls are operating effectively.
findings.detail: Planning (Service Standards) audit is marked Final (Sep 26) with Partial assurance. Partial assurance indicates that some control objectives are not being met. This audit covered 13 days of work.
findings.matters: Partial assurance in planning controls is relevant because delays or control failures in planning can impact the council's income and strategic project delivery.

findings.committee: Business and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget Monitoring at Quarter 1 (April to June 2026)
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £75.7m carrying forward to 2027/28, with delays cited in flagship schemes
findings.detail: The council is reprofiing £75.671m of capital spend to the next year. Delays include the West Cumbria Learning Centre replacement, Children's Care Homes purchase timelines, and notably 'delays in contracts being awarded' and 'dangerous buildings affecting works' on Town Deal and Carlisle Station Gateway schemes. These are not routine slippage but scheme-level delivery risk.
findings.matters: Capital programme delays often signal either procurement challenges, planning/governance risk, or underestimated project complexity. When multiple major schemes slip, it points to a systemic delivery issue, not isolated delay. Lenders fund capital plans; slippage affects timing of economic benefit and debt service.
findings.figures: £75.671m carry forward to 2027/28, £85.834m total underspend against £310.272m budget, £11m+ still to deliver in fleet replacement
findings.quote: A number of factors are contributing to this position, including delays in contracts being awarded, dangerous buildings affecting works, and the reprofile of the Cumberland Sports Village to align capital budgets to the project plan.

findings.committee: Business and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget Monitoring at Quarter 1 (April to June 2026)
findings.headline: Sustained demand-led pressure in children's services and agency staffing costing £12.5m in-year
findings.detail: Children & Family Wellbeing Directorate is forecasting £12.496m pressure, driven by Home to School and SEND transport, Cared for Children, and continued use of agency staff (EPW costs). This is a demand pressure, not a one-off, and is explicitly noted as a 'significant financial challenge' the council faces.
findings.matters: Structural demand pressures in statutory children's services are not easily cut; agency staffing is expensive and often temporary; councils under sustained pressure in this area often see it worsen before improving.
findings.figures: Children & Family Wellbeing £12.496m pressure; EPW agency staffing noted as key driver
findings.quote: Pressures, mostly in the Children & Family Wellbeing Directorate (£12.496m), associated with demand pressure in Home to School & SEND Transport and Cared for Children, and continued staffing pressures associated with EPW Agency costs.

findings.committee: Business and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget Monitoring at Quarter 1 (April to June 2026)
findings.headline: Planned corporate savings of £5.4m are not materialising on schedule
findings.detail: The council forecast an adverse variance of £5.417m from its transformation and savings programmes. Key programmes in trouble are 'Our Future Cumberland' and 'Customer Pre-Front Door', both showing timing or delivery issues. The council notes that in-year savings from a voluntary redundancy scheme have not yet been factored into Q1 forecasts.
findings.matters: Savings plans that slip in the first quarter often do not recover, and the council is already absorbing a £3.7m shortfall; a further £5.4m of undelivered savings compounds the pressure on reserves already breached.
findings.figures: £5.417m adverse variance on corporate savings delivery
findings.quote: An adverse variance of £5.417m relating to non-delivery or timing of corporate savings programmes, particularly: Our Future Cumberland, Customer Pre-Front Door

findings.committee: Business and Resources Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget Monitoring at Quarter 1 (April to June 2026)
findings.headline: General Fund reserves falling below the minimum adequacy threshold after unplanned Q1 draw
findings.detail: The council must contribute £3.719m from General Fund balances to cover Q1 overspend, reducing reserves to £24.965m against a stated minimum adequacy level of £25.000m. This is a material breach of the council's own floor on working capital, leaving no buffer for further in-year pressures.
findings.matters: A council operating below its minimum reserve threshold has reduced financial resilience and signals stress early in the financial year, with nine months remaining.
findings.figures: General Fund reserves to £24.965m, minimum adequacy level £25.000m, unplanned contribution £3.719m
findings.quote: The draft outturn position requires an unplanned contribution from General Fund balances of £3.719m. This takes General Fund reserves to £24.965m (subject to audit), which is below the Councils minimum adequacy level of £25.000m.

findings.headline: PMO Handbook still references governance board disbanded in February 2025, creating confusion about oversight responsibilities
findings.detail: Page 16 of the PMO Handbook references the Assurance and Efficiency Delivery Board (AEDB), which held its final meeting on 13 February 2025 and was disbanded in May 2025. Functions have transferred to the Strategic Programme Panel, but the handbook has not been updated. The audit recommended formal periodic review of the handbook to keep governance structures current.
findings.matters: Outdated governance documentation creates ambiguity about who is responsible for capital decisions and oversight, undermining the clarity and consistency of control over a £300m+ portfolio.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: This framework continues to reference the Assurance and Efficiency Delivery Board (AEDB), which was disbanded in May 2025, with its final meeting held on 13 February 2025.

findings.headline: Q3 2025/26 financial reporting obscures true reprofiling scale by showing revised budgets instead of original approved budgets
findings.detail: The Q3 report shows only £24m reprofiling (£209M revised budget vs £185M outturn), but this masks that total reprofiling is £185m against the original full-year budget of £371m. A reader of Q3 in isolation would not recognise that the council is underspending by nearly 50% against approved plans.
findings.matters: Transparent reporting of actual vs. approved spending is essential for lenders and the council's leadership to assess true financial position and capital delivery risks; misleading comparisons undermine decision-making.
findings.figures: 25/26 Q2: £371M budget; 25/26 Q3: £209M revised budget vs £185M outturn (showing £24M variance); total cumulative reprofiling £185m
findings.quote: The reporting position is potentially misleading, as the 2025/26 Q3 report reflects the revised budget following Q2 reprofiling, rather than the original budget approved at the start of the financial year... total reprofiling amounts to £185m, with projected expenditure representing less than 50% of the original budget.

findings.headline: Capital spending decisions are not formally documented; approvals are communicated by email with no recorded rationale
findings.detail: Capital Budget Growth Bids, Capital Reprofiling Requests, and Capital Saving Submissions contain no formal record of whether they were approved or rejected, who approved them, or why. The audit found: 'Management stated that outcomes are typically communicated directly to the relevant Directorate via e‑mail. As a result, the decision trail is not captured within the bid submissions themselves.'
findings.matters: Without documented decision trails, it is impossible to verify compliance with governance requirements, challenge questionable decisions, or hold leaders accountable for £300m+ in capital spending.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: There is no formal evidence recorded within the Capital Budget Growth Bid documentation to indicate whether a bid has been approved or rejected, and by who. Management stated that outcomes are typically communicated directly to the relevant Directorate via e‑mail.

findings.headline: No formal organisational capacity assessment has been done despite external auditors' explicit warnings of insufficient capacity
findings.detail: The audit found 'no evidence to demonstrate that a formal assessment of organisational capacity was undertaken' when £12.6m was reprofiled in May/June 2025. CIPFA explicitly recommended the council 'undertake a capacity review' but this has not been completed. The programme lacks 'a comprehensive resource mapping framework' to identify whether services have the people and skills to deliver 300 active projects across 98 programmes.
findings.matters: Without documented evidence that the council has sufficient capacity and capability to execute a 300-project portfolio, there is no assurance that approved capital will actually be delivered or that the spending will achieve intended outcomes.
findings.figures: approximately 300 active capital projects across around 98 programmes; £12.6m (4.2% of budget) reprofiled in May/June 2025
findings.quote: There is no evidence to demonstrate that a formal assessment of organisational capacity was undertaken reducing assurance that the revised programme is fully deliverable within available resources.

findings.paper_title: Risk Management Progress Report - Appendix 1 Risk in Focus Review - SRR-08 Financial Sustainability - Review Schedule 02 Period 02
